articleTitle: Advances in fault diagnosis using analytical redundancy
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Plant Optimisation for Profit (Integrated Operations Management and Control) (Digest No.1993/019)
abstract: This paper provides an overview of the subject of model-based fault diagnosis (fault detection and isolation) using analytical redundancy. Most of the recent advances and developments in this subject have been outlined, with a particular emphasis on robust design problems. The main principle is to use a residual, a symptoms of process faults to facilitate the diagnosis tasks. The residual is generated using the mathematical model of supervised process. A crucial goal of the residual generator design is to make the residual insensitive to modelling errors, whilst sensitive to faults. The best solution to this problem is to combine together disturbance decoupling design and the adaptive threshold decision-making. The methods outlined are very well suited to process control systems, particularly when robustness techniques are included.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: New developments in supply chain and factorywide management control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Plant Optimisation for Profit (Integrated Operations Management and Control) (Digest No.1993/019)
abstract: The emergence of computer networking technologies, the fall in the cost of computing power and the establishment of EDI technologies, has produced a world wide interest in computer integrated manufacturing (CIM), and in the management of multisupplier multi-user supply chains. The increased cost of finance and of inventory has resulted in a need for reductions in the considerable capital tied up in inventory in many supply chains. Furthermore the increasing need for improved customer service and the need to supply the right products at the right time and in the right place, essentially means that supply chains are being operated under EDI, on much faster dynamic time scales and hence the need for new control procedures. The dynamic behaviour of most warehouses and retail operations are relatively simple, compared with that of manufacturing activities, and hence in seeking to tightly control the network, there is a need for improved operation within the manufacturing activity. Hence there is a special interest in factory wide control from a supply chain viewpoint. The main interest of this discussion will be centred around the theme of decision support system design. These systems deal with cost-sensitive decisions which radically effect the efficiency of the business and the customer service level.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Optimisation and management control in the paper industry
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Plant Optimisation for Profit (Integrated Operations Management and Control) (Digest No.1993/019)
abstract: The article concerns 3 optimisation problems from the paper industry. They require different techniques. They are the cutting stock problem (short-term), the scheduling problem (medium-term), and the problem of product cycles (long-term).<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: An application study of integrated system optimisation and parameter estimation (ISOPE) algorithms using the OTISS dynamic plant simulator
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Plant Optimisation for Profit (Integrated Operations Management and Control) (Digest No.1993/019)
abstract: The need for improving the online adjustment of process operating conditions has long been recognised as an important issue of plant operation and management in the chemical process industry. In order to address this need, substantial research into improving existing optimisation algorithms has been performed during the last decade; this has lead to significant improvements in robustness and accuracy. The increased availability of low cost high power computers has improved the feasibility of applying online optimisation; and this, coupled with advances in dynamic modelling techniques, has at last made the technology a practical tool.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A framework for integrated operations management and control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Plant Optimisation for Profit (Integrated Operations Management and Control) (Digest No.1993/019)
abstract: Lasdon and Baker (1986) introduced a framework for plant wide online hierarchical control as an integration of planning, scheduling and process control. A hierarchy is proposed consisting of six layers; strategic planning, tactical planning, systems operations planning, plant operations planning, scheduling, and process control. In the context of this paper, integrated operations management and control is a subset of plant wide control and is concerned with integrated operations management, control system coordination, and assessment. These three functions are arranged within a functional multilayer hierarchy which is considered to be operating on top of a distributed computer control system (DCS) regulating an industrial process plant complex. Here, the integrated operations management unit perform the system and plant operations planning functions of the Lasdon and Baker hierarchy, and the control system coordination unit performs the lower two functions of short term scheduling and process control. The strategic and tactical planning functions are, for the time being, considered to be outside the current considered framework but provide production goals as input. However, an additional function of assessment is introduced within the framework. The system is analysed.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Integrative approaches to production planning and control
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Plant Optimisation for Profit (Integrated Operations Management and Control) (Digest No.1993/019)
abstract: The importance of integrating the various problems and models, which constitute in their totality a production planning and scheduling system, is argued. It is also argued that such integration is now feasible due to increasing computerisation, and that hierarchical planning provides the natural framework for integrative approaches. The paper presents, in outline, and discusses four hierarchical systems. The paper also compares and contrasts the integrative hierarchical approach with that of material requirements planning (MRP), to conclude that although the former appears more amenable to realising crucial planning objectives, the two can, in fact, be regarded as complementary.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
